words.text: A cloth is the picture your machine weaves on the loom, stitch by stitch. Every cloth you finish goes into your journal.

Your journal keeps everything you've learned and made: the paints, how the loom keeps time, what every piece does, your inventions, the cloths you've woven and your best scores. Its pages fill as you play.

The loom weaves your cloth. Every tick it takes one drop from its tube and weaves it into the next stitch, row by row, left to right. If a stitch doesn't match the picture, the loom stops and shows where.

There are eight paints. Red, yellow and blue mix into all the others: red and yellow make orange, and all three together make black. No paint at all is white, the bare cloth. More of the same paint changes nothing.

The paint card shows all eight paints at a glance. Red, yellow and blue sit at the corners, each mix sits between the two paints it's made of, black is in the middle and white sits apart. Opposites face each other across black. Tap Paints to put it up or away.

A piece is anything you take from the tray and put in the workshop to build your machine. Every piece has a cost, and the lower your machine's cost, the more stars it earns. Machines you invent become pieces you can use again.
The red pot makes red paint: a new drop whenever its tube is free. Every other paint in the box starts from this one pot.

The shuttle is the little wooden boat that carries thread across the loom. It marks the stitch the loom weaves next, and slides on after every stitch lands. A pattern card has one too, marking the drop that comes next.

Every cloth you weave earns stars: one for weaving it, two for a machine with a low cost, three for the lowest cost anyone can make it for. Your journal keeps your best stars, your lowest cost and your fewest ticks for every level.
A stitch is one square of a cloth. The loom weaves one stitch from each drop it takes, row by row, left to right. If a stitch comes out wrong, the loom stops and shows you which one.
A thread is one line of stitches in a cloth: a row across, or a column down. The paint box's cloths are single threads.

A tick is one beat of the workshop clock. On every tick, each piece that has paint waiting at every input, and room to send its paint on, does its job once. A pattern card lets out its next drop and the loom weaves one stitch. The clock counts the ticks until your cloth is done: fewer ticks, faster machine.

The tray along the bottom holds the pieces you can use. Drag one into the workshop, or tap it to pick it up. A piece with a lock is one this level does without. Your pots share one slot: tap it and they fan out above the shelf, then drag one out. To put a piece away, drag it back onto the tray.
A glass tube carries paint from one piece to the next: from the spout on a piece's right to the pipe on another's left. A tube holds one drop at a time, so the next drop waits until it's free.

The workshop is where you build. Put pieces in it from the tray and join them with tubes. Paint comes in from the pattern cards on the left, flows to the right, and the loom on the right weaves it into a cloth.

Critters are the workshop's little helpers. Each one does one job to paint: paint drips in on its left, it does its job, and the new paint comes out on its right. A critter always does the same thing to the same paint, so once you know it, you can count on it.
Solve some levels and the machine you built becomes an invention: one piece you can use again, cheaper by one than the pieces inside it. Every paint-box level earns a pot of its paint.

The Shift Wheel turns paint one step round the wheel: red becomes yellow, yellow becomes blue, and blue becomes red again. Mixed paints turn too: orange becomes green. White and black stay as they are.

cases.why: Everything in either one.
Red is there already, so nothing changes.
Between them they hold red, yellow and blue.

words.text: The Mixing Tub takes two paints and gives back everything in either one. Red and yellow make orange; orange and blue make black. Mixing in a paint that's already there changes nothing.
Split copies paint: one drop goes in, and the same paint comes out of both spouts. It's free, so it never counts toward your pieces.

In a real paint box, red, yellow and blue stirred together make a muddy brown. Here they make black, so brown gave its place to black. It didn't go far: it's the wood of every tub, bench and shelf in the workshop.
The Flip Pan flips a paint to its opposite. Red becomes green, yellow becomes purple, blue becomes orange, and white becomes black. Flip it again and you're back where you started.
Weave every cloth in a chapter and they're sewn together into a quilt. Your quilts hang beside your cloths in the journal.

A pattern card holds a picture as paint, one drop for every stitch, laid out like the cloth: left to right, row by row. It lets its drops out one at a time, in order; the ones already let out fade, and a little shuttle stands before the one that comes next. Tube it to a piece, or straight to the loom.

cases.why: Red is all they share.
They share nothing, so nothing gets through.
Black has everything, so the other paint gets through whole.

words.text: The Sieve takes two paints and keeps only what they share. Orange and purple share red, so out comes red. Two paints that share nothing give white.

cases.why: Blue is the one neither has.
What both have doesn't matter; blue is still missing.
The same paint twice gives its opposite.
White has nothing, so out comes the other paint's opposite.
Between them they have everything, so nothing is left.
Neither has anything, so out comes everything.

words.text: The Third Paint mixes two paints and gives back the opposite: whatever neither of them has.

cases.why: They share nothing, so it's a plain mix.
The red they share washes out.
The same paint twice shares everything, so nothing is left.
White brings nothing, so nothing changes.
With black, any paint turns into its opposite, as on the Flip Pan.
With blue, blue comes out if it was there and goes in if it wasn't.

words.text: Extreme Mix mixes two paints, but whatever they share washes out.

cases.why: They share red; yellow and blue are each missing from one of them.
They share nothing, so everything is missing from one or the other.
The same paint twice gives its opposite.
White lacks everything.
Black lacks nothing, so out comes the other paint's opposite.

words.text: Missing From Either gives whatever one paint or the other lacks: the opposite of what the Sieve keeps.

cases.why: The same paint twice agrees on everything.
They agree only on lacking blue.
Both have red and both lack blue; they disagree on yellow.
With black, a paint stays as it is.
With white, a paint turns into its opposite.
Opposites agree on nothing.

words.text: Same Paint keeps what two paints agree on: what both have and what both lack.
